newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Vranitzky aims to lead govt through CA minefield.
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky aims to lead govt through CA minefield.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky said on Tuesday political dissent over the sale of the nation's second biggest bank Creditanstalt was straining relations in the coalition government.

Rightist politicians have rallied to prevent "socialist" Bank Austria from taking control of Creditanstalt, its roots set deep in conservative tradition, and have raised the spectre of a repeat of last year's snap general election.
"This is certainly a grave topic...(but) I believe this government is doing a good job and I will do my utmost to hold it together," Social Democrat Vranitzky told journalists.
"I believe we can solve the problem. There is no reason to cast doubt on the government," he continued.

The conservative People's Party has accused the Social Democrats, the senior coalition partner, of engineering Creditanstalt's renationalisation through Bank Austria, which is effectively controlled by the City of Vienna.

"I have made my position absolutely clear. It remains to be seen whether the finance minister accepts it," conservative Economy Minister Johann Farnleitner said. "Privatisation means selling to private individuals."

Finance Minister Viktor Klima, a Social Democrat, has vowed to name a buyer for the state's 70 percent of Creditanstalt ordinary voting shares by the end of the year. Farnleitner pressed for a decision by the end of the week.
Klima has three options: Bank Austria, an international consortium headed by Italian insurer EA-Generali or former supermarket mogul Karl Wlaschek, 79.

Analysts say Klima may have difficulty rejecting Bank Austria's offer, reportedly worth some 16-17 billion schillings to depleted state coffers. At current market prices the government's holding is worth 14.5 billion.
The EA-Generali group, publicly favoured by the People's Party, has bid around 14 billion schillings while Wlaschek has put together 13-15 billion, according to Austrian newspapers.

The EA-Generali consortium, which includes "conservative" savings bank Die Erste Oesterreichische SparCasse (First Austrian), Germany's Commerzbank, and Italy's Banca Commerciale Italiana, has been circling Creditanstalt since 1994.
Bank Austria and Wlaschek emerged as late bidders in the drawn-out, six-year privatisation that entered the home stretch on Monday when the deadline for final bids passed.

Vranitzky said he was confident Klima would fulfil the task set him by parliament -- maximising revenues, safeguarding Austrian interests and contributing to a long-overdue restructuring of the domestic banking sector.
"We must arrive at a sensible, economic solution that makes sense in banking terms," Vranitzky said.
Relations between the coalition partners have deteriorated recently after a brief post-election honeymoon.

People's Party general secretary Maria Rauch-Kallat accused the Social Democrats and Bank Austria of concealing the bank's planned bid for Creditanstalt. "They lied to us...this is not the way to behave in a coalition," she said.
Bank Austria's attempted coup has also drawn fire from Creditanstalt employees, fearful for their jobs, and conservative business groups wary of losing their power base.
"An intelligent and forward-looking solution would be a buy-out by Creditanstalt workers, supported by their customers," said Werner Fasslabend, a People's Party minister.
